candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — warfarin pharmacogenetics and INR monitoring
candidate.educational_objective: Explain the limited but useful role of warfarin pharmacogenetic information while preserving the requirement for INR-guided dosing.

options.A: Genotype information can help inform the initial warfarin dose, but the dose still must be individualized and adjusted using INR monitoring and clinical factors
options.B: That is correct; once CYP2C9 and VKORC1 are known, INR monitoring is no longer necessary
options.C: Genetic results are used only to determine blood type and have no relationship to warfarin dosing
options.D: Genotype results determine a fixed lifelong dose that should not be changed for medications, diet, illness, or INR results

candidate.rationale: Warfarin dose requirements vary with clinical and genetic factors. Current labeling states that known CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes may be considered when choosing the initial dose, but therapy still requires close INR monitoring and subsequent individualized dose adjustment. Genotype does not define a fixed dose or replace monitoring.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CYP2C9/VKORC1 information can inform initial warfarin dosing but does not replace INR-guided individualized therapy.
candidate.source_document_title: Warfarin Sodium / COUMADIN — Full Prescribing Information
candidate.source_locator: Sections 2.3–2.4 — initial dose influenced by clinical and CYP2C9/VKORC1 genetic factors; if genotype known consider dose ranges; determine ongoing needs with close INR monitoring
candidate.stem: A client starting warfarin has CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotype results available and says, ‘Since the genetic test tells my provider what dose I need, I will not need INR checks.’ Which response by the nurse is best?
